Limaçon. A limaçon, the French word for snail, is a rose-like curve defined in polar coordinates, famous for its variety of shapes depending on a parameter. The cardioid is a special limiting case of this family. More generally, limaçons display either a single loop or an inward dimple, appearing frequently in rose-pattern problems and mechanical curves.

The equation is simple in polar coordinates: r equals a plus b cosine theta, or with sine for rotated versions. The curve's shape depends entirely on the ratio of b to a. When b equals a, the curve becomes a cardioid. When b is less than a, the curve is convex. When b is greater than a, an inner loop appears. The name captures the resemblance to a snail's shell and spiral motion. Blaise Pascal first studied the limaçon, though full recognition of its properties came later with systematic polar coordinate analysis. The curve is closed and smooth except in the loop case at the origin, and it has beautiful aesthetic appeal and symmetry properties. When b equals half of a, the curve is a dimpled limaçon with a smooth inward curve. When b equals two a, the loop becomes prominent. Limaçons have practical applications in antenna design, optics, and mechanical transmission curves, making them more than just pretty patterns—they're curves that actually appear in engineered systems.
